idiom_name: SwiftRuleEngine: {path, operator, value} conditions in JSON
implementation_notes: Swift has no platform rule engine, so the declarative option is a library such as SwiftRuleEngine: rules are JSON-shaped dictionaries whose conditions are all/any trees of {path, operator, value} leaves evaluated against a decoded input, and operators are extensible through the Operator protocol (a custom operator is a small struct with a static id and a match(_:) method). Rules therefore travel as data - config files, server-provided JSON - while operators remain typed Swift code, which is the useful split: new thresholds need no build, new kinds of comparison do. Adoption is small, so wrap it behind your own rule-evaluation protocol.
pitfalls: Conditions address the input through JSON paths: a renamed field or wrong path makes a condition silently false (or throws), so rule JSON needs schema validation and tests.
Rules are [String: Any] dictionaries with no type information: typos in operator names surface at evaluation time and each operator's value shape is its own contract.
The library is small and has no agenda, salience or cross-fact matching - treat it as a condition evaluator, not as a production rule system.

variants.name: Foundation predicate composition
variants.implementation_notes: The platform-provided realization composes predicates instead of running an engine: predicates are combined with NSCompoundPredicate's AND/OR/NOT constructors (or, since Swift 5.9, written with the type-checked #Predicate macro, which can be converted to NSPredicate), and a rule is such a predicate plus the action the caller performs when it evaluates true. Conditions stay compile-checked and dependency-free, but there is no agenda, chaining or rule store - the rule set is Swift code and changes with the app. Choose it when the rules are stable enough to ship in the binary and composing them is the valuable part.
pitfalls: NSCompoundPredicate rules are strings evaluated with key-value coding: an invalid key path raises an Objective-C exception rather than a Swift error, so predicate strings from outside the binary are both unsafe and hard to debug.
The predicate language can call methods on the evaluated object: predicate text carries the privileges of the process, so it is code, not configuration.
Composed predicates have no conflict resolution or chaining - when two rules match, precedence is whatever the calling code imposes, which must therefore be explicit.
